newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Change NZ CPI measure, not inflation band - Smith.
newsitem.headline: Change NZ CPI measure, not inflation band - Smith.

text.p: Calls for changes to Reserve Bank inflation target ranges by the Labour Party and New Zealand First could have only short-term benefits, caretaker Agriculture Minister Lockwood Smith said on Tuesday.

"The perceived benefits of expanding the target range could be short-term and might be out-weighed by the medium term downside," Smith said in a speech prepared for the annual meeting of the Dairy Board in Wellington.
"If the Reserve Bank were to be given greater latitude, it is likely that that latitude would be used," he said.

"A wider target range would lead to higher average inflation over time and higher interest rates," Smith said. There would be more uncertainty about money and decision-making by businesses and individuals would become more difficult.
"I believe we are better to look at changes not to the inflation target range but to how the CPI is measured."

Nationalist New Zealand First is currently in coalition negotiations with both the main opposition Labour Party and the caretaker National Party in the quest to form a new government after October 12's inconclusive general election.
Labour wants to keep the one percent mid-point for the Reserve Bank's inflation target, but to expand the range to minus one to three percent.
New Zealand First wants inflation kept below the trade-weighted average of major trading partners, which was around 3.5 percent last year.

Smith said the frequency of breaches of the target range would not change if the RBNZ had a more flexible goal. "And the frequency of the need for a response would not change. But the responses would need to be more severe," he added.

The distance from the one percent inflation mid-point would be greater and the damage to the credibility of the price stability goal would create greater inflationary expectations, requiring a stronger response.
Smith said his main concern about the impact of coalition negotiations on the dairy industry were over fiscal policy.
It was inevitable government spending would increase with MMP, but the question was by how much.

"It would be disastrous for New Zealand and New Zealand exporters if the price of a new government under MMP was a pledge to attempt to control inflation in the face of unrealistic increases in Government spending," Smith said.
"The best way to win elections is to spend money," he said.
"The problem is $50 million more each Monday at cabinet may not sound much to some politicians. If a government fails to resist the temptation, New Zealand no longer has a surplus.

"All parties need to keep in mind that extra spending will put pressure on inflation, and will mean that the Reserve Bank will need to run a tighter monetary policy...with higher real interest rates and a higher dollar."
Smith said the good news was that in coalition talks last week New Zealand First had lectured Labour about Labour's "unsustainable fiscal commitments".
